overview: Canaan here means a region of Bronze Age cities and villages, with different local rulers, rather than one kingdom or nation. The atlas assigns it one broad outline from about 2000 to 1500 BCE, stretching across the southern Levant into the Lebanese coast. That outline cannot show each city’s changing territory. This card follows excavated communities at Aphek, Laish, Kabri, Megiddo, Jericho and Lachish; its dates do not mark the beginning or disappearance of all Canaanite cultures.

periods.title: Cities and regional rulers
periods.summary: Middle Bronze towns expanded, built defenses and exchanged goods with Egypt and neighboring regions.

periods.title: Palaces, crafts and households
periods.summary: Fortified centers supported elaborate crafts and storage. Local archaeological chronologies differ, so these are broad regional phases.

periods.title: Changing regional power
periods.summary: The transition toward the Late Bronze Age brought political changes; Egyptian dominance developed in Canaan while local communities continued.

items.text: At Aphek, beside the Yarkon springs, excavators identified a Middle Bronze palace, successive fortifications and burials inside the settlement. Egyptian Execration texts also name Aphek and its ruler Ya’nakilu. Buildings and an external written record together reveal a local royal center, rather than a capital governing all Canaan.

At ancient Laish, now Tel Dan, a mudbrick gateway dating roughly to the early second millennium BCE preserves three arches, four rooms and steps. Its impressive entrance shows builders organizing space and loads with brick long before the familiar stone arches of Roman monuments.

Laish’s surrounding embankment reached roughly 10 to 15 meters high and 60 to 70 meters across its base. The gate was blocked only decades after construction, according to the site guide. An expensive building could change its job surprisingly quickly; an ancient city was a work in progress.

One Middle Bronze house at Megiddo, Building 12/K/15, is estimated to have housed 10 to 15 people. Over about 150 years, at least 45 individuals were buried beneath its floors. The ages at death fit an extended-family pattern, although that interpretation does not establish everyone’s biological relationship.

The Megiddo household treated its dead in different ways: graves varied in construction, objects and later reopening. Some burials were revisited while others remained undisturbed. Archaeologist Melissa Cradic interprets those choices as ways of maintaining family memory within a home shared by successive generations.

A clay loom weight excavated at Jericho, dated by the Carlos Museum to 2000 to 1600 BCE, makes clothing production tangible. Surviving tools and scraps reveal textile work even where whole garments have vanished. A small, unglamorous lump of clay can tell us more about work than a royal statue.

The Jericho textile display describes draped robes and kilts fastened with toggle pins, alongside less common tunics sewn into shape. Clothing required making thread and fabric before fitting a garment. The museum treats several proposed fibers and loom arrangements as reconstructions, not a surviving instruction manual.

Ancient tooth deposits can keep an unexpected menu. A person buried at Megiddo between about 1688 and 1535 BCE had wheat and sesame proteins preserved in dental calculus. Researchers studied these microscopic traces in hardened plaque; the evidence records food contact, not a complete lifetime diet.

Another Megiddo individual, dated about 1630 to 1550 BCE, yielded proteins identified as soybean and turmeric. Such foods support connections reaching toward South Asia. This is evidence from particular people and exchange networks, not proof that every family could buy imported spices at the nearest stall.

sections.title: Palace stores and archaeological detective work

items.text: At Kabri in western Galilee, excavators uncovered about 40 large jars in one Middle Bronze palace storeroom. Most held roughly 50 liters and lacked handles. These were serious containers: shifting a full one was not a one-handed trip to the cupboard.

The Kabri team tested residues from 32 jars and kept eight untested for future comparisons. Chemical markers supported the identification of grape wine. Empty pottery thus preserved a trace of what a palace stored and served, long after the liquid itself disappeared.

Other Kabri compounds suggested resins and possible flavorings, though not every proposed ingredient can be pinned down. The fairly uniform jars used locally available clay materials. The room joins two kinds of expertise: making reliable containers and preparing beverages for an elite establishment.

Before removing the Kabri jars, archaeologists recorded the room with laser scanning. Millions of points produced a plan accurate to about two millimeters. Modern technology helped preserve where the ancient pots lay, information that lifting them out would otherwise disturb.

sections.title: Grooming and a tiny written wish

items.text: A small ivory comb found at Lachish had six coarse teeth for untangling hair and fourteen fine teeth for removing lice and eggs. The teeth had broken in antiquity. Under a microscope, researchers found a tiny surviving membrane from a louse nymph: an unwelcome passenger with remarkable staying power.

The comb bears this published Roman transcription of early Canaanite alphabetic writing: ytš ḥṭ ḏ lqml śʿ[r w]zqt. Its editors translate: “May this tusk root out the lice of the hai[r and the] beard”. Brackets mark restored damaged letters. They propose about 1700 to 1550 BCE from letter forms; the object came from a much later pit, so its precise date remains uncertain.

The comb’s wish is readable but still debated: scholar Bob Becking interprets one word as “inscription” rather than “tusk”. Its practical purpose is clear, while the wording raises questions about whether writing itself was thought to help the grooming tool do its work.

Kabri’s palace was abandoned around 1700 BCE in a revised archaeological chronology. A 2020 study found rapid collapse and several kinds of possible earthquake damage. Its authors propose that a quake helped make the complex unusable; this is a local explanation under investigation, not a single disaster ending all Canaan.

The Kabri investigators combined large features, including a trench through the palace, with microscopic evidence from fallen building materials. Their approach asks how a ruin formed before naming its cause. Broken walls are clues, but identifying an earthquake requires more than noticing that something fell down.

ending.text: The atlas stops this label at 1500 BCE, not at the disappearance of Canaan’s inhabitants. Cities followed different paths into the Late Bronze Age as Egyptian power expanded; local crafts, households and exchange continued under changing political conditions.
